title: SQL and database systems

spans.text: “SQL and database systems” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.

spans.code:
SQLite: app.db file
MySQL / PostgreSQL: client program -> database server

spans.text: SQLite is file-based; MySQL and PostgreSQL commonly use a client-server architecture.

SQL is a query language, not a database. SQLite, MySQL, and PostgreSQL are database management systems (DBMSs) that accept SQL. The SQLite project began in 2000; it needs no separate server and stores data in a file, so it is used in mobile and desktop apps, browsers, and devices. MySQL emerged in the 1990s and became common for web applications and servers handling many concurrent connections. PostgreSQL began as the POSTGRES project at Berkeley in 1986, led by Michael Stonebraker; SQL was added to the project in 1994, and the PostgreSQL name was adopted in 1996. It is used for server and analytics workloads requiring extensive SQL features and reliability. The systems share core SQL ideas, but data types, functions, administration commands, and some syntax differ.

Key line: `SQLite: app.db file`
What it does: SQLite often runs inside the application; MySQL and PostgreSQL commonly run as separate server processes.
Why it is used: Choose an engine by checking whether you need a server, concurrent writes, and the required operational features.
If omitted or changed: SQLite is an open-source, serverless library/engine; MySQL and PostgreSQL are server systems that can serve many network clients.

spans.title: Common mistake
spans.text: The SQL standard does not guarantee identical behavior across engines; check dialect differences and migrations when switching.
